title: Tokenizer, prompt architecture, and routing profiles — POC notes
content:
Context and goal:
This doc captures hands-on findings from the field POC with a mid-size commerce customer that needs a language-intent router + slot-filling pipeline. Primary constraints: multi-lingual (en/es/fr), 95th-percentile latency <= 220ms for short requests, and a token-cost budget to hit a target spend. Focus areas for this sprint: tokenizer choice impact on prompt length, how tokenization interacts with quantized model behavior and KV-cache efficiency, and practical routing profile heuristics we can ship as part of the pilot.

Summary of actionable conclusions (short):
- Choose Unigram SentencePiece for this customer: best balance of stable token counts across en/es/fr and robust subword splitting for short prompts.
- Prefer group-wise 4-bit (G4) quant for Mistral-style variants when throughput matters; fall back to 8-bit rowwise on Llama-family for better fidelity on rare token sequences.
- Align prompt templates to token boundaries (don’t insert arbitrary whitespace tokens) and standardize a 3-token separator to maximize prefix-KV cache hits.
- Implement a routing fingerprint based on the first 12 token ids (hashed) + language detection; this gives >90% deterministic routing to the same model variant across repeated user utterances.

Detailed observations and experiments:
1) Tokenizer experiments (BPE vs SentencePiece Unigram vs WordPiece)
- Setup: 10k-sample production-ish corpus split across en/es/fr (conversational + titles + product descriptions). Measured avg tokens per user prompt, token-length variance, and percent of prompts that exceeded 512-token working window.
- Results: Unigram had the lowest variance and ~8–12% fewer tokens on short chatty prompts vs WordPiece. BPE (model-trained) gave slightly smaller token counts for long product descriptions but was brittle across languages.
- Practical impact: Token-count variance directly changes both cost and KV-cache hit probability. For our prefix-caching scheme, 1 extra token of variance reduced hit rate by ~4%.

2) Tokenization <-> Quantization interactions
- Observation: Under aggressive 4-bit PTQ on Llama-like weights, we saw subtle but measurable degradation on rare-token completions (proper nouns, SKU-like tokens). Mistral-like models with per-group scaling were less sensitive.
- Diagnostic: Activation distributions for the early layers shifted for certain subword IDs (rare suffixes) after quantization. These shifts propagate and affect sampling for low-probability tokens.
- Mitigation tried: per-token calibration (re-scaling logits for a small blacklist of tokens) helped recover some accuracy but cost complexity; instead we default to using higher-precision variants for critical routes (e.g., order-id parsing).

3) KV-cache alignment and prompt slicing
- Problem: When we dynamically inject or template few-shot examples, tokenization differences (leading spaces vs explicit separators) broke cache reuse because cached prefixes were tokenized differently.
- Fix: Define canonical separators ("\n\n<SEP>\n\n") that are normalized before tokenization. Strip trailing spaces from all template variables to avoid invisible tokens.
- Result: Cache hit rate improved from ~58% to ~77% across the evaluation set; end-to-end latency dropped 18% for medium-length prompts.

4) Routing profile design (fast/cheap/accurate lanes)
- Approach: Create three routing lanes per customer profile: fast (low-precision small model), balanced (medium precision/size), and high-fidelity (higher precision larger model). Routing keys: language, tokenized-prefix fingerprint, intent-probability (classifier), and SLAs (latency budget).
- Fingerprint design: first 12 token ids hashed with an XOR-shift + low-bit mod to bucket into 256 route buckets. This is stable across sessions if tokenizer is canonicalized.
- Observed behavior: Deterministic routing using tokenized prefix reduces user-facing jitter (model variance) and simplifies cache warm starts for dedicated pools.

5) Prompt template experiments and few-shot engineering
- Templates: compared single-shot vs two-shot vs compressed exemplars (where exemplar context is compressed via extractive summaries).
- Findings: For this customer, 1 compressed exemplar + schema constraints (JSON schema in system prompt) outperformed 2 raw exemplars for both throughput and quality. Compression reduced tokens by ~40% compared to raw few-shot while keeping F1 on slot extraction within 2 points.

Metrics and benchmarks (representative):
- Baseline: llama-7b unquantized (reference)
- G4-Mistral-16k-variant: 4bit-GW quantized, avg latency 95ms (p50), p95 190ms; token-cost 0.62x baseline; slot extraction F1 = 0.88 vs baseline 0.91.
- Llama-7b-8bit-rowwise: avg latency 110ms (p50), p95 230ms; token-cost 0.78x; slot F1 = 0.90.
- Prefix-KV caching effect: for repeated conversational context, effective tokens sent to model reduced by 25–40% depending on prompt churn.

Decision log (what we recommend for the pilot):
- Tokenizer: Ship Unigram SentencePiece with canonical normalization hooks in the client SDK.
- Quantization profile: Default to group-wise 4-bit on Mistral-like variants for the balanced lane. For high-fidelity lane use 8-bit rowwise on Llama variants. Provide explicit model labels in routing metadata so the runtime can select the right kernel.
- Prompt architecture: standardize separators, avoid leading/trailing whitespace in variables, compress exemplars by default, use schema constraints for extraction tasks.
- Routing: implement token-prefix fingerprinting + language code; keep fast lane conservative (no G4 on Llama).

Open questions and risks:
- Does Unigram generalize to new languages (de, nl) if the customer expands regionally? We should run a small tokenization sweep before wider rollout.
- Rare-token precision: need a policy for when to prefer 8-bit variants for specific routes — should be SLO-driven (latency vs correctness).
- Operational complexity: maintaining per-route quantization constraints increases serving variants; evaluate cost of extra model variants in Dedicated pools.

Next steps and experiment checklist (short-term):
- Add canonicalizer into SDK: strip/normalize separators + tokenization sanity checks (owner: Miguel, JIRA-SE-1976).
- Run a 20k-sample sweep on DE/NL if pilot stakeholder asks for EU expansion (owner: Leah).
- Add a per-route override flag in the routing policy to force high-fidelity lane for regex-matched SKUs/order-ids (owner: Omar).
- Trial automatic exemplar compression routine in the prompt builder and measure F1 delta on slot extraction (data engineer + SE).

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc mixes lab numbers and early field telemetry; treat the numeric results as directional.
- If we proceed with Unigram tokenizer as default, we should check compatibility with existing customer token accounting (billing) and document any differences in per-token metering.

Appendix: quick checklist for the SW rollout (developer handoff)
- SDK: expose tokenizer normalization toggle (boolean) and canonical separator constant.
- Runtime: tag model artifacts with quantization metadata (G4, 8bit-RW, PTQ/QAT) so routing can reason about fidelity automatically.
- Ops: pre-warm dedicated pools for the fingerprint buckets that are hot (top 25% by volume) to improve p95 latency.

End of notes.

-- Evelyn (SE lead)
